meta.method: deterministic rule-based analysis, rules documented in docs/ADVISOR_METHODOLOGY.md
meta.note: findings are computed from the data on every rebuild; with different data these findings change, including to no action justified

findings.title: Treatment upsets (hours of poor COD removal)
findings.problem: The plant sometimes stops cleaning properly. We flag any stretch of 3 hours or more where COD removal stays below 75 percent. We use cleaned baseline data.

evidence.summary: 6 upsets, totalling 54 hours below 75 percent COD removal. About 1794.0 kg of extra COD was discharged. That is measured against the plant's own normal removal of 88.5 percent. The high-severity threshold is 500 kg.
details: 2026-07-19T05:00:00 to 2026-07-19T16:00:00: 12 h. Removal fell to 54.8 percent at worst. About 353.9 kg of extra COD left the plant. That is measured against the normal (median) removal of 88.5 percent, applied to the same incoming water.

2026-07-22T02:00:00 to 2026-07-22T05:00:00: 4 h. Removal fell to 58.0 percent at worst. About 87.8 kg of extra COD left the plant. That is measured against the normal (median) removal of 88.5 percent, applied to the same incoming water.

2026-07-29T05:00:00 to 2026-07-29T13:00:00: 9 h. Removal fell to 58.8 percent at worst. About 310.9 kg of extra COD left the plant. That is measured against the normal (median) removal of 88.5 percent, applied to the same incoming water.

2026-07-30T01:00:00 to 2026-07-30T12:00:00: 12 h. Removal fell to 54.3 percent at worst. About 470.0 kg of extra COD left the plant. That is measured against the normal (median) removal of 88.5 percent, applied to the same incoming water.

2026-08-11T19:00:00 to 2026-08-12T02:00:00: 8 h. Removal fell to 56.5 percent at worst. About 268.9 kg of extra COD left the plant. That is measured against the normal (median) removal of 88.5 percent, applied to the same incoming water.

2026-08-20T20:00:00 to 2026-08-21T04:00:00: 9 h. Removal fell to 55.3 percent at worst. About 303.0 kg of extra COD left the plant. That is measured against the normal (median) removal of 88.5 percent, applied to the same incoming water.

Incoming strength check: median influent COD was 646.0 mg/L during upsets. Outside upsets it was 643.0 mg/L. The difference is +0.6 percent. We only call the influent 'unusually strong' above +10 percent.

possible_causes.cause: The incoming water was not unusually strong during the upsets. Median influent COD was 646.0 against 643.0 mg/L. So stronger influent does not explain them.
The treatment microbes (biomass) may have been stressed or poisoned. This needs measurement.
Aeration or other equipment may have failed during those hours. This needs checking.
Short-lived toxic compounds may have entered with the influent. COD alone cannot show this.

findings.recommendation: Write a simple upset response procedure. Trigger it when COD removal stays below 75 percent for 3 hours. Steps: confirm the readings with a hand sample. Check aeration and dosing equipment. Note the influent source at the time. Do the measurements listed below before buying anything. The current data cannot tell the possible causes apart.
validation_required: Measure dissolved oxygen in the biological stage. The dataset has none.
Examine the biomass under a microscope during and after an upset. The dataset has none.
Screen the influent for toxic or inhibiting compounds. The dataset has none.

findings.title: Sensor health, per instrument
findings.problem: Sensors can give bad readings. We check each sensor column with the record's tags plus our own checks. We look for missing values, impossible values, and identical repeats of 3 hours or more (stuck sensor). A sensor fails when over 0.3 percent of its readings are bad.

evidence.summary: All 9 sensor columns are below the 0.3 percent limit. We found 21 bad readings in total across 2880 hours.
details: influent_flow_m3h: 2 bad readings out of 2880 (0.069 percent). The limit is 0.3 percent. By check: impossible_low 2. Worst month: 2026-07. Examples: 2026-07-20T13:00:00, 2026-09-29T14:00:00.
influent_ph: 1 bad readings out of 2880 (0.035 percent). The limit is 0.3 percent. By check: missing 1. Worst month: 2026-10. Examples: 2026-10-27T16:00:00.

influent_cod_mgl: 5 bad readings out of 2880 (0.174 percent). The limit is 0.3 percent. By check: missing 2, spike_above_range 2, impossible_low 1. Worst month: 2026-08. Examples: 2026-08-05T09:00:00, 2026-08-24T18:00:00, 2026-08-25T05:00:00.

influent_tss_mgl: 5 bad readings out of 2880 (0.174 percent). The limit is 0.3 percent. By check: missing 1, stuck 4. Worst month: 2026-07. Examples: 2026-07-14T17:00:00, 2026-07-14T18:00:00, 2026-07-14T19:00:00.
effluent_ph: 2 bad readings out of 2880 (0.069 percent). The limit is 0.3 percent. By check: spike_above_range 2. Worst month: 2026-09. Examples: 2026-09-01T20:00:00, 2026-10-05T02:00:00.

effluent_cod_mgl: 6 bad readings out of 2880 (0.208 percent). The limit is 0.3 percent. By check: stuck 6. Worst month: 2026-07. Examples: 2026-07-13T14:00:00, 2026-07-13T15:00:00, 2026-07-13T16:00:00.
No bad readings in: influent_bod_mgl, effluent_bod_mgl, effluent_tss_mgl.
The record's own tags show: {'missing': 4, 'out_of_range': 3, 'sensor_spike': 4, 'sensor_stuck': 10}. Our checks and the tags are counted separately. One reading can trip more than one check.

findings.recommendation: No sensor needs attention now. Keep the checks and routine calibration running. Bad readings are already removed before any KPI is computed.

findings.title: Always-on electricity use (base load)
findings.problem: Some electricity is used no matter how much water flows. We fit a straight line: kWh = a + b x flow. The intercept (a) is the always-on part, called base load. We flag it when base load is over 15 percent of average hourly use.

evidence.summary: Base load is only 0.7 percent of average hourly use. The limit is 15 percent. Electricity tracks flow well (R2 = 0.914).
details: Fitted on 2789 cleaned normal hours.
Always-on part (intercept a): 1.06 kWh per hour.
Flow-linked part (slope b): 0.7929 kWh per m3. Fit quality (R2): 0.914.
Average use: 154.1 kWh per hour. Base-load share: 0.7 percent. The limit is 15 percent.
An intercept near or below zero means effectively no base load in this data.

findings.recommendation: No investigation needed now. Re-run this check when new data arrives. Submeter the big drives if a finer breakdown is ever wanted.

findings.title: Coagulant dose and what it buys (dose response)
findings.problem: We test whether more coagulant actually buys better solids removal (TSS removal). We use cleaned normal hours. We compare removal at the highest doses against the lowest doses (top against bottom quartile). A difference under 1.0 percentage point counts as no visible response.

evidence.summary: Solids removal does not change with dose in this data. Dose range tested: 57.6 to 62.4 g/m3 (middle half). Quartile difference: -0.13 percentage points. Correlation: -0.019. The data cannot say why.
details: Computed on 2789 cleaned normal hours over 120 days.
Dose spread: P25 57.6, median 60.1, P75 62.4 g/m3.
Link (correlation) between dose and TSS removal: -0.019.
Top dose quarter: 93.46 percent removal. Bottom quarter: 93.59 percent. Difference: -0.13 percentage points. The limit for 'no response' is 1.0 point.

possible_causes.cause: Removal does not vary with dose across the doses actually used.
Dosing may already be past the point of diminishing returns (saturation plateau). The top of the range would then be wasted.
A real response may be hidden by noise and the narrow dose range.

findings.recommendation: Run a controlled stepped-dose trial first. Vary the dose on purpose. Sample the effluent at each step (jar tests plus TSS samples). This separates a real plateau from noise. No dose reduction is justified today. The saving below applies only if the trial confirms the plateau.

expected_impact.summary: If the trial confirms a plateau: trim doses above the median down to the median. That saves about 2305.0 kg of coagulant a year. The figure comes from the actual dose record.

calculations.label: trim target: median dose, base case

assumptions: The trial must confirm no loss of TSS removal at the trimmed doses. Without that, there is no saving.
Savings use cleaned normal hours, scaled to a year by calendar days (x 365/120).
We assume this period's influent and dosing represent a full year.

sensitivity.description: Trim target at the P60 (low), P50 (base) and P40 (high) dose percentile. A lower target trims more and saves more.

findings.tradeoffs: Cutting coagulant without trial evidence risks losing solids removal. The whole saving depends on the trial outcome.

quality_gate.check: A stepped-dose trial must show TSS removal is unaffected at the trimmed doses.
quality_gate.note: This gate cannot pass on the current data. No reduction is justified today.

validation_required: Run the stepped-dose trial with jar tests and effluent TSS samples. The dataset has none.
Keep coagulant batch quality records for the trial period.

findings.title: Effluent pH control
findings.problem: Treated water should leave at a near-neutral pH. We count cleaned hours outside pH 6.5 to 7.8. Under 20 such hours in 120 days, the check is cleared.

evidence.summary: 0 hour(s) outside pH 6.5 to 7.8, out of 2859 cleaned hours. That is below the 20 hour limit.
details: Observed effluent pH range: 6.8 to 7.6.

findings.recommendation: No action needed. Effluent pH is well controlled over this period.

findings.title: Missing measurements (data gaps)
findings.problem: Some measurements are missing from this dataset. The gaps limit how far the other checks can go. Nothing is invented to fill them, and the simulation is not extended.

evidence.summary: 5 measurement gaps found by checking the dataset's columns. Several causes in R1 to R4 stay unproven until these are measured.
details: Dissolved oxygen in the biological stage. Why it matters: Without it, upsets (R1) cannot be traced to aeration, overload or poisoning. What to measure: Log dissolved oxygen in the aeration basin every 15 minutes.

Blower and aeration power submetering. Why it matters: The energy check (R3) sees one total meter. The biggest consumer cannot be separated. What to measure: Submeter the blowers and other big drives. Log them hourly.

Controlled dose-response trial data. Why it matters: The dose check (R4) cannot tell a plateau from noise without deliberately varied doses. What to measure: Run a stepped-dose trial with jar tests across a wider dose range.

Design capacity and equipment ratings. Why it matters: Loads cannot be judged against design limits. Headroom and overload risk are unknown. What to measure: Record nameplate capacities and design flows next to the operating data.

Laboratory-verified samples. Why it matters: Online COD, TSS and pH readings are never checked against lab values here. What to measure: Take periodic lab samples paired to timestamps. Use them to audit the online instruments.

findings.recommendation: Add these measurements before committing to equipment or dosing changes. They turn the hypotheses in the other findings into testable evidence.
validation_required: Log dissolved oxygen in the aeration basin every 15 minutes.
Submeter the blowers and other big drives. Log them hourly.
Run a stepped-dose trial with jar tests across a wider dose range.
Record nameplate capacities and design flows next to the operating data.
Take periodic lab samples paired to timestamps. Use them to audit the online instruments.
